content.title: Volume of Prisms, Cylinders, Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres
content.overview: This guide covers the volume calculations for three-dimensional geometric figures commonly found on the SAT. The focus is on mastering the volume formulas for prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres, and understanding the relationship between base area and height.
learning_objectives: Identify and apply volume formulas for prisms and cylinders
Distinguish between and apply volume formulas for pyramids and cones
Calculate the volume of a sphere
Solve for dimensions (such as radius or height) given the volume of a figure

sections.title: Prisms and Cylinders
sections.content: The volume calculation for prisms and cylinders follows the same basic principle: the area of the base ($B$) multiplied by the perpendicular height ($h$). For a prism, the base can be any polygon; for a cylinder, the base is a circle. The formula is $V = Bh$. For a cylinder, since the base area $B = \pi r^2$, the formula is specifically $V = \pi r^2h$.

sections.title: Pyramids and Cones
sections.content:
The volume of pyramids and cones is one-third the volume of a prism or cylinder with the same base and height. The formula is $V = \frac{1}{3}Bh$. For a cone, the base area $B = \pi r^2$, so the volume formula is $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$. Note that $h$ must be the perpendicular distance from the vertex to the base, not the slant height.

![Volume Formula Classification](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/5b130104-b893-4bde-b079-55cc46451028-1786502091102-753.webp)

sections.title: Spheres
sections.content: The volume of a sphere depends only on its radius ($r$). The formula is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. On the SAT, a problem might provide the diameter; in this case, you must divide by 2 to get the radius before substituting it into the formula.

worked_examples.question: A cone has a height of 9 cm and a base diameter of 6 cm. Find the volume of the cone in terms of $\pi$.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Determine the radius. $r = \text{diameter} / 2 = 6 / 2 = 3$ cm. Step 2: Apply the cone volume formula $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$. Step 3: Substitute the values, $V = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \pi \cdot (3)^2 \cdot 9$. Step 4: Calculate, $V = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \pi \cdot 9 \cdot 9 = 27\pi$ cubic centimeters.

worked_examples.question: A rectangular prism has a volume of 120 cubic units. If the base area is 30 square units, find its height.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Use the formula $V = Bh$. Step 2: Substitute the known values, $120 = 30 \cdot h$. Step 3: Solve the equation, $h = 120 / 30 = 4$. The height is 4 units.

common_mistakes: Using the diameter instead of the radius when calculating the volume of a cylinder or cone.
Forgetting to multiply by $1/3$ in the formulas for pyramids or cones.
Squaring the radius ($r^2$) instead of cubing it ($r^3$) when calculating the volume of a sphere.
Confusing perpendicular height ($h$) with slant height; volume calculations must use perpendicular height.
exam_tips: Basic geometric formulas are usually provided at the beginning of the SAT Math sections; you can refer to them if you are unsure.
Pay attention to unit conversions; although the SAT rarely tests complex unit conversions in volume problems, you should still note the required units for the answer.
If the question asks for an 'exact value,' it usually means leaving $\pi$ in the answer; if an approximation is required, use 3.14 or the $\pi$ key on your calculator.
content.recap: The core of calculating volume lies in identifying the figure category: use $V=Bh$ for prisms/cylinders, $V=\frac{1}{3}Bh$ for pyramids/cones, and $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ for spheres. Always ensure you use the radius rather than the diameter and the perpendicular height for calculations.

knowledge_claims.content: The general volume formula for all prisms and cylinders is the base area ($B$) multiplied by the perpendicular height ($h$), or $V = Bh$.
The volume formula for a cylinder can be specifically expressed as $V = \pi r^2h$, where $r$ is the radius of the base.
The volume formula for pyramids and cones is one-third the volume of the corresponding prism or cylinder, or $V = \frac{1}{3}Bh$.
The volume formula for a cone is $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$, where $h$ is the perpendicular height.
The volume formula for a sphere is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.
When calculating volume, if the diameter is given, it must be halved to find the radius before substituting it into the formula.
When calculating the volume of a pyramid or cone, the perpendicular height from the vertex to the base must be used, not the slant height.
If two cylinders have the same height but different radii, the ratio of their volumes is equal to the ratio of the squares of their radii.
If the volume and base area are known, the height of a prism or cylinder can be calculated using $h = V / B$.
Given the same base area and height, the volume of a cylinder is 3 times the volume of a cone.
